title: ITPD Learns Nonstationary Causal Graphs 40x Faster
summary: Cornell Tech, Abel AI, and Arizona State released ITPD, a constraint-based algorithm for causal discovery on time series that runs 40.9x faster than PCMCI.
body_markdown:
#### 💡 TL;DR


- Cornell Tech, Abel AI, and Arizona State released ITPD, running 40.9x faster than PCMCI on 2,000-node graphs with F1 scores above 0.997.
- ITPD maintains F1 0.984-0.994 on nonstationary graphs where edges change over time, outperforming PCMCI, DYNOTEARS, and CD-NOD by 30-40 points.
- The team published machine-verified soundness and completeness proofs in Lean 4.3, using AI-assisted autoformalization with Claude, GPT-6, and Gemini.


Cornell Tech, Abel AI, and Arizona State University researchers have released Iterative Temporal Parent Discovery (ITPD), a constraint-based algorithm for causal discovery on multivariate[time series](https://emergent.sh/glossary/time-series-analysis) that handles nonstationary causal relationships. Officially released on November 21, 2026, the method ran 40.9 times faster than PCMCI on 2,000-node graphs while maintaining F1 scores between 0.997 and 0.998, according to a Hugging Face paper published today.


The team describes ITPD as the first sound and complete constraint-based procedure of its kind for this setting. Lead author Jacqueline Maasch of Cornell Tech collaborated with Shu Wan, Hank Zhu, and Zhiguang Wang of Abel AI, plus Huan Liu of Arizona State.


## Performance on Large Stationary Graphs


On 2,000-node graphs with stable causal relationships, ITPD demonstrated speed improvements across multiple baselines. The algorithm ran 2.3 times faster than iterative IAMB, 9.1 times faster than DF-PC, and 40.9 times faster than PCMCI. All methods held F1 scores in the 0.997 to 0.998 range, indicating ITPD achieved accuracy parity with dramatically reduced runtime.


The local-to-global structure of the algorithm enables parallel discovery of temporal parent sets, contributing to the speed gains. The authors note that ITPD scales efficiently as graph size increases, a critical property for real-world applications involving hundreds or thousands of observed variables.


## Nonstationary Causal Relationships


ITPD's core advantage emerges on nonstationary graphs where causal relationships shift over time. In experiments where 5% of edges were randomly redrawn at each timestep, ITPD held F1 scores between 0.984 and 0.994. Competing methods, including PCMCI, DYNOTEARS, and CD-NOD, scored between 0.562 and 0.808 on the same benchmarks.


The 30 to 40 percentage-point gap reflects ITPD's explicit handling of causal nonstationarity. Traditional constraint-based methods assume causal relationships remain constant across time, an assumption that breaks in many real-world domains such as financial markets, climate systems, and adaptive biological networks.


## Machine-Verified Proofs and AI Assistance


The research team published soundness and completeness proofs formalized in Lean 4.3, a theorem-proving language. The proofs appear in Appendix D of the paper and were developed with AI-assisted autoformalization using Claude, GPT-6, and Gemini.


Formal verification eliminates ambiguity in correctness claims. The authors disclosed the specific AI tools used in the proof process, a transparency practice that remains uncommon in machine-learning research. The Lean formalization provides a mechanically checkable guarantee that ITPD satisfies its theoretical properties under the stated assumptions.


## Limitations and Domain Constraints


The paper explicitly identifies scenarios where ITPD does not outperform alternatives. On DREAM4 gene regulatory networks at early timesteps with 200 observations, PCMCI, CD-NOD, and DYNOTEARS outperformed ITPD. The authors cite a lack of public real-world benchmarks as a direct limitation on their evaluation.


ITPD assumes no contemporaneous links between variables at the same timestep and no latent confounding after the first timestep. These restrictions simplify the causal-discovery problem but may not hold in all applied settings. The team suggests future work could relax these assumptions while preserving computational efficiency.


## Release Date


The ITPD paper was officially released on November 21, 2026, and is available on Hugging Face. The release includes code, benchmark datasets, and the Lean 4.3 proof artifacts.


## What This Means


ITPD extends causal-discovery methods to nonstationary settings where relationships evolve over time, a gap in existing constraint-based approaches. The 40x speedup over PCMCI on large graphs and 30-point F1 improvement on nonstationary benchmarks suggest ITPD could enable causal analysis on larger, more dynamic systems. The machine-verified proofs and disclosed AI-assistance workflow set a methodological standard for transparency in algorithm development. For practitioners working with time-varying causal systems, ITPD offers a formally grounded alternative to methods that assume stationarity.
